REGRESSION LOSS FUNCTIONS
==========================

Loss functions measure how wrong a regression model's predictions are.

Example
-------
Actual delivery times:     10, 20, 30
Predicted times:           12, 17, 36

Error = Actual - Predicted:
2, -3, 6


1. L1 LOSS
----------
L1 uses the absolute value of each error.

Absolute errors:
|2|, |-3|, |6| = 2, 3, 6

L1 Loss = 2 + 3 + 6 = 11

Meaning:
How much total are the predictions wrong?


2. MEAN ABSOLUTE ERROR (MAE)
----------------------------
MAE is the average of the absolute errors.

MAE = (|y1 - y_hat1| + ... + |yn - y_hatn|) / n

For our example:

MAE = (2 + 3 + 6) / 3
MAE = 3.67

Meaning:
On average, the predictions are wrong by about 3.67 minutes.

MAE stays in the original unit, so it is easy to understand.


3. L2 LOSS
----------
L2 squares each error and then adds them.

Squared errors:
2^2, (-3)^2, 6^2 = 4, 9, 36

L2 Loss = 4 + 9 + 36 = 49

The important point:
Large errors become much larger after squaring.

Error:       2    3    6
Squared:     4    9   36


4. MEAN SQUARED ERROR (MSE)
---------------------------
MSE is the average of the squared errors.

MSE = sum((y - y_hat)^2) / n

For our example:

MSE = (4 + 9 + 36) / 3
MSE = 16.33

MSE gives much more importance to large errors.


5. ROOT MEAN SQUARED ERROR (RMSE)
---------------------------------
RMSE is the square root of MSE.

RMSE = sqrt(MSE)

For our example:

RMSE = sqrt(16.33)
RMSE ~= 4.04

Why take the square root?

MSE has squared units. If delivery time is measured in minutes:

MAE  -> minutes
MSE  -> minutes^2
RMSE -> minutes

So RMSE is easier to interpret in the original unit while still penalizing large errors more than MAE.


THE WHOLE FAMILY
----------------

                         ERROR
                           |
              +------------+------------+
              |                         |
              v                         v
          Absolute                   Squared
            error                     error
              |                         |
              v                         v
           L1 Loss                    L2 Loss
              |                         |
              v                         v
           Average                    Average
              |                         |
              v                         v
             MAE                       MSE
                                          |
                                          v
                                     Square root
                                          |
                                          v
                                        RMSE


QUICK SUMMARY
-------------

L1 Loss  -> Absolute errors -> Add
MAE      -> Absolute errors -> Average

L2 Loss  -> Squared errors  -> Add
MSE      -> Squared errors  -> Average
RMSE     -> Square root of MSE

Remember:

MAE:
"On average, how many units am I wrong?"

MSE:
"How much do large errors hurt me?"

RMSE:
"How large is my typical error in the original unit, while still penalizing large errors more than MAE?"


CONNECTION TO LINEAR REGRESSION
-------------------------------

Ordinary Linear Regression is commonly based on minimizing squared errors
(least squares). That is why MSE/L2 appears frequently when learning
Linear Regression.

For evaluation, we can use MAE, MSE, or RMSE depending on what we want
the metric to tell us.
